title_en: Diplomats race to compromise on fossil fuels as Cop31 teeters on brink of failure – as it happened
excerpt_en: EU thought to have backing of 130 countries in last-ditch push to get cause of climate crisis mentioned in outcome of UN summit
body_en: Day 13 of Cop31 – recapped That’s all for today – we hope everyone following from Antalya gets a good night’s sleep. Here are the highlights from the 13th day of the 31st UN climate summit, which is still not over:
Activists told the Presidency this summit could be one of the ‘ most disappointing Cops ’ ever
Carbon removal must ‘ be additional, not a substitute ’ for phasing out fossil fuels, a top scientist said
‘ We will not allow obstruction to dampen our resolve,’ Tuvalu’s climate minister said
The EU was thought to have the backing of 130 countries to get fossil fuels back into the draft text
Diplomats raced to find compromise as the joint presidencies held meetings with scores of countries
A plenary session gavelled through a handful of less controversial decisions, but the Presidency pushed the big day till Sunday
Cop31 President, Murat Kurum, ended the day by announcing a new draft would be with delegates “shortly”, ahead of a new plenary at 9am local time.
Thanks for following – stay tuned for more.
“Today we have listened to you and sought to find common ground for your expectations,” said Murat Kurum, thanking the tired delegates for their “constructive approach”.

He said the third and final version of the cover decision will be “in your hands shortly”, and parties will have until 6am local time to consider the text, before plenary reconvenes at 9am. The text is currently being scrutinised by the lawyers of the secretariat, he said.
“The political will needed to complete this bridge is present in this room,” he said, declaring the end of the meeting.

Cop31 President, Murat Kurum, has arrived on the main stage, and has been immediately swarmed by delegates. The Turkish-Australian joint presidency has kept a low public profile today, on the first day of overtime, and the transparency they promised has been somewhat hard to come by for observers of the process. Still, as my colleagues have reported on this blog, they have been busy trying to find compromise between different parties.
A handful of less controversial topics have indeed gone through without issue, and the session is taking a brief break before the Cop31 President arrives.

A dispute has broken about gender – and how it is defined – with interventions from Argentina and Paraguay. The draft document “encourages” a finance committee to enhance efforts to ensure gender-responsiveness in implementing its workplan, and requests Parties to consider gender balance and geographical representation when nominating members.

This is not the first time the issue of gender has cropped up in climate negotiations. In previous years, a handful of countries have voiced objections to gender definitions that do not refer to biological sex.

Next up is a text on long-term climate finance, which has been rejected by the African Group. “This process did not provide sufficient space for negotiations,” said the negotiator for Ghana, speaking on the group’s behalf. “For now, it is not ready on our side for adoption.”

The objection is to paragraph 3, which “notes with appreciation” a report on progress towards (belatedly) achieving the goal of mobilising $100bn per year to address the needs of developing countries “in the context of meaningful mitigation actions and transparency on implementation”.
The EU, right after Ghana’s intervention, has said it “cannot accept changes to the text as we have already shown significant flexibility”.
This does not seem to be the smooth ride we were hoping. The chair has just proposed we come back to the decision later in the meeting.

The plenary session has now actually begun, and we understood that it’s only the uncontroversial topics that are to be gaveled through. However, the very first topic, on climate empowerment – helping all members of society engage in climate action – has been met with an immediate objection from Russia that has drawn consternation from other countries. The EU, echoed immediately by the UK, next expressed “surprise and disappointment” at the objection. Panama, speaking on behalf of AILEC – 8 Latin American and Caribbean countries – echoed this.
On account of the objection, the chair has requested the SBI consider the decision at its next session.

title_en: Two groups verify mathematician’s claim that Claude helped prove mathematics problem
excerpt_en: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis
body_en: A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics – and experts say the claim checks out.

Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.
On Saturday afternoon, two organizations announced that they had independently verified Alpöge’s claim after reviewing the programming language he used to share the solution.

The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems.
Related: Anthropic’s historic stock market debut: key takeaways, and what comes next for the AI industry

“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
Alpöge linked to computer code – written in a language called Lean – that he maintained could verify the findings.

Mathematicians subsequently began working to see if Alpöge’s proof could be confirmed. On Saturday afternoon, the Lean Focused Research Organization – which seeks to advance the use of the programming language – and the Mathlib Initiative, a program that works with Lean for math equations, announced that they had verified Alpöge’s solution.
“We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” the groups announced.

Alpöge’s note was published just one day after Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq stock market index. He acknowledged that, writing: “The precise timing is horrible. If I could have, I’d have finished this all much earlier.”
The Riemann hypothesis is a nearly 170-year-old math problem named after Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician who proposed it in 1859.

The hypothesis deals with prime numbers – whole numbers greater than 1 that can only be divided by themselves and 1. Riemann questioned how often prime numbers appear and how they are distributed along the number line. And he developed a formula for estimating how many prime numbers exist under a specific number.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium prize math problems selected in 200 by the Clay Mathematics Institute. The institute has offered $1m for each problem solved.

Mathematicians have been attempting to solve this problem for years. The New York Times reported that on Friday, an independent mathematician in Italy released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he said he had been working on for almost 12 years. That mathematician, Alessandro Masullo, said he did not use AI because he did not fully trust the system.
Other mathematicians have expressed discomfort with relying on AI to solve math problems.

In September, Anthropic competitor OpenAI claimed that a non-public version of its AI tools helped solve part of another Millennium prize problem. But it was solved in a way that struck mathematicians and observers in a way many found strange: a near-trillion-dollar private company spent $15m to employ 10,000 AI systems to solve the problem.
Alpöge was working on that separate problem for Anthropic when OpenAI made its announcement.

University of Warwick mathematician James Robinson told the Guardian in September that “it’s frustrating to see these big tech companies burning this fuel up just so that they can show off about how great their latest model is”.

He added: “It seems like immature playground boasting writ large, underpinned by billions of dollars and the potential for significant environmental damage in an age when climate change is probably the biggest challenge we face.”

title_en: Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology?
excerpt_en: The post Why Is the World Still Counting on Unproven Carbon Capture Technology? appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Supporters of the climate movement Fridays for Future protest in Berlin on Nov. 13. Ralf Hirschberger/AFP/Getty Images You see the promise on airline booking screens, shipping boxes, electronics and grocery aisles: “Carbon neutral.” “Net zero.” “Climate pledge friendly.” Those labels rest on the comforting premise that even when companies and countries keep burning fossil fuels, the resulting pollution can be canceled out by simply capturing the carbon and locking it away.

Recently, along with my colleagues at ProPublica and Drilled, I investigated how the world came to rely so heavily on this premise, particularly in the technology known as carbon capture and storage. CCS aims to trap carbon dioxide that would otherwise be warming the atmosphere and pump it thousands of feet below Earth’s surface, where, ideally, it stays put. The oil industry has long favored the idea.
At the industry’s prodding, the United Nations has effectively endorsed the idea that the technology can work at a massive scale.

Over the last two weeks, world leaders and negotiators met in Antalya, Turkey, for the U.N.’s annual flagship climate summit, where nations hash out global commitments to curb warming. A central foundation of these negotiations — and many of those carbon-neutrality labels and climate pledges — is the expectation that we can bury billions of tons of CO2 a year, an operation that would rival today’s entire global oil industry within just a couple of decades.

Yet our reporting found that expectation rests on thin evidence. After three decades of development, only 12 large-scale geologic storage projects have ever been built, and at least seven have underperformed or failed. Last year, the world buried less CO2 underground than a single large power plant emits annually.
Why do world leaders keep staking climate policy on a technology that remains unproven?
Because the models they all rely on to guide their approach have already presumed that it will work.

I spoke to more than 100 experts for this series, including several members of the wildly powerful group of people who build and run those models. Their simulations of the economy and environment map out how specific choices, like retiring coal plants or electrifying vehicles, could prevent warming catastrophic enough to submerge cities like Miami. Which means that if they’re wrong, Miami could pay the price.

One chart laid bare to me exactly how wrong they’ve been about CCS. It compares one prominent model’s projections for CCS with their projections for solar power, a technology so abundantly tested and proven that you can likely spot a panel out the nearest window:
Carbon Capture Capacity Has Never Come Close to Projections Meanwhile, solar electricity production has grown rapidly, far outpacing projections.

Note: The modeled pathways, what we call projections, for deployment of carbon capture and storage are from text and tables in the International Energy Agency’s Energy Technology Perspectives and World Energy Outlook reports, and from correspondence with the IEA. Lucas Waldron/ProPublica I wanted to understand what could possibly account for such a disparity. But the problem is the models are opaque: Unlike most scientists, who trade in public, peer-reviewed studies, modelers aren’t required to document every assumption they build into their influential simulations.
So I tracked down the leaders of the world’s three most influential climate models — one based in the Netherlands, another in Germany and a third in Austria — and asked. Here’s what I learned:

Climate models assume it’s easy and efficient to capture carbon. It’s not. Public data is hard to come by, but several analyses have found the real capture rates are far lower than the industry has promised. Yet the models calculate as much as a 92% success rate. When I pointed out this discrepancy to Keywan Riahi, who leads the Austrian model, he insisted that capturing concentrated CO2 from industrial emissions “is not high-tech, this is very easy to do.” Riahi told me the models assume a high rate of capture because they factor in incentives such as payouts from carbon taxes and large government subsidies. Add those incentives, he argues, and the capture rates would increase.

They don’t account for problems that come up in real-world practice. In project after project, operators have struggled to inject as much carbon into the earth as they say they can. For instance, at Chevron’s Gorgon natural gas processing plant in Australia, billed as the largest CCS operation on Earth, clogged wells and pressure spikes have forced operators to release most of their CO2 straight into the air. As it stands, only the German model, led by Jessica Strefler, assumed there’d be any limit to how much CO2 operators could inject underground at once. But, she told me, there is no good data to work from, and she pegged the limit based on “expert interviews” with people in the industry.

They assume the Earth is a bottomless geologic landfill. Modelers took that cue from a rosy 2005 U.N. report, which I’d learned had been written at the behest of Saudi Arabia and allied petrostates, that portrayed underground storage space as practically limitless. (The U.N.’s climate science body has said it stands by the report. Scientists who contributed to the report also defended their work. Authors and editors from Saudi Aramco, Chevron and Shell joined scientists in writing it; the companies did not respond to requests for comment.) Yet just last year, a paper in the journal Nature warned that the earth’s capacity to absorb CCS could be far more limited once you rule out pumping the gas beneath cities, into earthquake zones and under the deepest parts of the oceans. If CCS ever worked at the scale modelers imagine, the paper found, the Earth could run out of room as soon as early next century. Riahi, himself a co-author on that paper, conceded that although his model presumes the earth’s capacity for carbon storage is literally infinite, the real potential may be “smaller.”

title_en: Alleged Mexican drug cartel boss ‘El Chapo Isidro’ arrested in special forces raid
excerpt_en: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores was one of FBI’s most wanted fugitives and evaded capture for more than a decade
body_en: The Mexican military captured one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives during a special forces raid in the Mexican state of Sinaloa on Friday night.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was arrested along with two other alleged leaders of his gang after a gun battle that triggered widespread panic in the city of Guasave.

The alleged leader of a major drug-trafficking cartel, the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization (TCO), he had managed to evade arrest for more than a decade, even though there was a reward of up to $5m (£3.8m) on his head.

His FBI “most wanted” poster states his organisation “is allegedly responsible for the possession, distribution and importation of large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl and marijuana into the United States, and has predominately controlled drug production, transportation and distribution in several locations throughout Mexico”.
Mexico’s defence ministry also alleged he is the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organisation, which is allied to the Mayos, one of two rival factions in the powerful Sinaloa cartel.
Meza Flores’s alleged second-in-command, Germán N, whose alias is “Serafín”, and José N, an alleged financial operator for the Beltrán Leyva group, were also arrested.
The operation to capture the men was carried out by “elite military forces” with help from US intelligence, according to Mexico’s defence ministry.

After arriving in the “target area … using stealth and surprise”, the ministry said the arresting force came under attack “with gunfire and explosives” but managed to enter a house and make the arrests.
The men were then evacuated to Mexico City on a Mexican air force plane to be handed over to prosecutors.
Videos and photos show civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game at Kuroda Park stadium in Guasave, as well as burnt-out cars.

A barrage of rapid fire from what appeared to be Mexican security force helicopters hit the ground, according to CNN, and players from the Venados de Mazatlán and Algodoneros de Guasave teams abandoned the field mid-game.
Four Mexican army infantry soldiers died in the operation, the defence ministry said in a statement posted on X that extended the institution’s condolences to their families.

It added that security forces killed seven attackers and arrested eight alleged criminals in the operation, including three who were transferred to Mexico City and five who were turned over to the attorney general’s office in Culiacán, Sinaloa.

Overnight on Friday the military operation triggered a wave of violence in the state of Sinaloa, including armed ‌clashes between Mexican security forces and cartel members, who ‌set up flaming roadblocks in some areas.
By Saturday the violence had substantially subsided. Sinaloa state authorities said “the situation is under control and being addressed by all levels of government”.
Meza Flores was originally indicted in 2012, and in 2013 the US Treasury placed sanctions on him under the Kingpin Act, freezing his assets.
In 2017, the US Department of State’s Narcotics Rewards Program began offering up to $5m as a reward for information leading directly to his arrest or conviction.

He has been charged with multiple counts of drug-trafficking violations, and use and possession of a firearm in the US, and was wanted in Mexico for organised crime and offences against public health.

title_en: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
excerpt_en: Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’
body_en: Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.

Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.

Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.

Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.

The US said the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.

South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a new law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.

The CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any new laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.

The Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, said world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”

Diplomats inside the negotiations said Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.

The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.

Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.

Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the issue of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.
One European diplomat said: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”

A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, said autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.
A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.

On Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”

title_en: Deniz Tek: ‘Top Gun may have got the name of Val Kilmer’s Iceman from me’
excerpt_en: The Radio Birdman guitarist on his time in the US Marines, selling a guitar to Keith Richards and getting texted by Anthony Albanese
body_en: Have you ever had a nickname, and what is it?

When I was in the US Marines F-4 Phantom squadron, Iceman was my call sign, which is given to you on your first operational deployment. You have it on your helmet and a patch on your flight suit. One day, a film crew came to visit our squadron, doing research for a film they were working on, and they hung out with us for two weeks.

A year and a half later, the movie comes out, and it’s Top Gun. The story got started that they got the name of Val Kilmer’s Iceman character from me. Most likely it was already written into the screenplay, but who knows? My squadron mates always say I’m the original Iceman.
Related: James Blunt: ‘Do I have a nickname? Yes, it rhymes with blunt’
Apart from buying and playing Fred “Sonic” Smith ’s guitar for your whole career, you once sold a guitar to Keith Richards. Tell us about that.

I lucked into getting into their inner circle when they were in Sydney in 1973. I was 20. I had a guitar, a 1958 National Baron. I knew Keith liked those guitars, so I rang up his guitar tech and asked him if he thought Keith might be interested in having it. He said, “Oh God yeah, bring it around after the show.” That guitar was my ticket to the top three floors of the Hyatt Kingsgate in Kings Cross. I hung out all night and had the most mind-blowing time. I wanted to trade the guitar for one of his, but that didn’t work out; he just gave me some money for it.
What album do you always return to, and why?

The first one that comes to mind is James Brown, Live at the Apollo in 1963. From the moment the needle hits the groove, it’s pure excitement – the Godfather of Soul in his early days, hitting his peak. Usually live albums are disappointing, I think, but that one’s not. It just jumps out and hits you like you’re right there.
Is it true that during your ER days in Newcastle, Australia, you delivered a baby by the name of Daniel Johns, later of Silverchair?

There’s a grain of truth to it, but it wasn’t Daniel, it was Chris [Joannou, Silverchair’s bassist]! I didn’t find that out until they invited me to record a cover of New Race with them in New York, and they asked me when I was doing obstetrics at the Mater. And that’s how I found out I was around when Chris was born. I don’t remember him as a baby specifically, but it’s definitely possible that I attended his birth.
You live in Hawaii and grow coffee on your own farm. What’s your coffee order?
When I’m overseas, it’s a cortado, and when in Australia, a piccolo.
What’s the oldest thing you own, and why do you still have it?
I have some fossils that are 60m or 70m years old, and I just keep them around because it’s cool to have something that you can hold in your hand that’s that old.

As far as something that I actually acquired, I guess it would be the T-shirt that Keith Richards gave me on that tour. And in those days, they didn’t have merch – there was no such thing as merch! – but their crew had tour T-shirts identifying what they did, and I asked for one of those.

Keith said, “Wait a minute,” and he goes over to his bag, and it was like this little carry-on. It was tiny, and he’s pulling out these amazing pieces of clothing. It was blowing my mind to even see this stuff. And he pulled out this T-shirt, and he says, “Here, you can have this.” It was a T-shirt from their 1966 tour of the United States.
What’s the weirdest thing you’ve ever eaten?
Ants on toast at a high-end restaurant in Melbourne. And I loved it!
Related: Ella Hooper: ‘Most embarrassing celebrity encounter? I said the classic thing you don’t ever say to Billy Bragg’
Who’s the most famous person in your phone?

Anthony Albanese. Before he was PM, he would sometimes come to our gigs. He’d text me if it was last minute and we were sold out. We always welcomed him backstage. He would chat with me, have a beer off the rider. He was a great supporter of the band, even in parliament.

After he became PM he still came to see us a couple of times, once at the Factory theatre in Marrickville and once at the Manning Bar. The security detail had to be accommodated, obviously. That coordination was done via our manager and the venues.

title_en: ‘Little room for error’: what a debt-laden cloud computing company says about the AI boom
excerpt_en: ‘Poster child of AI bubble’ CoreWeave symbolises increasingly risky business model of datacentre buildout
body_en: The Egyptians had pyramids. The Roman empire had roads. The early 21st-century tech bros have massive buildings full of expensive glass and metal blocks providing the substratum for a powerful inhuman intelligence.
Building all those datacentres is taking a while, locals everywhere are angry about them and it is unclear whether the inhuman intelligence inside them is actually going to make their backers rich.
This could be a problem for the people building those buildings – and therefore everyone else.
Almost no company is more exposed to the downsides of the AI boom than CoreWeave, a band of former crypto miners turned datacentre merchants, which has been called the poster child of the AI bubble.
The company sells the raw power for AI, known as compute, out of what it says is a network of 52 datacentres around the world, from Texas to Scotland.

Many of these are under construction; some are little more than announcements. CoreWeave is building them by taking on staggering quantities of debt. The company now owes $47bn (£36bn) and is borrowing more, with $10bn of this figure due next year. It bled $709m last quarter, on revenues of $3.6bn.
CoreWeave already looked dangerously exposed this autumn, when creditors put its risk of default – being unable to pay its debts – at over 60% at some point over the next five years.

Its earnings, released earlier in November, provided a brief respite from some of their fears – its margins and revenues “knocked it out of the park”, said Jordan Chaflin, head of technology at CreditSights, a financial research firm.

Interactive That was before scandal hit Nvidia, the most valuable business in AI and the company that makes CoreWeave’s entire business model possible. Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. He’s now out. This will have consequences, and no one knows what they are yet.
Huang ran his business on close relationships and, as Nvidia grew, these relationships became the scaffolding of the AI economy. Few companies will be more affected by his removal than CoreWeave.
Its vulnerabilities – and they are many – are a blueprint for the wobbly structure of the AI bubble itself, on which the fortunes of the world’s stock market and the global economy now depend.

A repository for other companies’ risk CoreWeave is what is called a “neocloud”. Its basic business model is this: the world’s biggest AI companies, like OpenAI, want billions of people to start using their products but don’t want to sink a fortune into building the large datacentres it takes to run them. Nvidia, its primary backer, wants to sell lots of computer chips to the world’s biggest AI companies.
So Nvidia provided the finance for CoreWeave and its peers to buy its chips, stuff them into datacentres, and rent that computational power to the world’s biggest AI companies.

Interactive Nvidia owns approximately 11% of CoreWeave. There are other arrangements, too, including a $6.3bn deal in which Nvidia agreed to buy “compute” that CoreWeave cannot sell – a sort of guarantee.

That’s not the only side of the equation Nvidia is propping up. It also has invested in CoreWeave’s clients – companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and nearly a dozen others that rent these chips. A dollar that Nvidia invests in one of these can end up as income on CoreWeave’s balance sheet, and then revenue for Nvidia as CoreWeave purchases chips.

Circular arrangements like this are the scaffolding of the AI economy. CoreWeave – and companies like it – are the vehicle through which Nvidia can make its balance sheet look spectacular, and OpenAI and Anthropic can provide ever-more-powerful models to their customers without paying workmen to break earth in Texas.

Think of it as a sandwich where neither slice of bread – Nvidia or a frontier AI company using its chips – wants to finance or build, say, $1tn worth of sheds stuffed with semiconductors, so the peanut butter in the middle takes on the risk.
Analysts expect CoreWeave to be a capital-intensive – meaning big-spending – business. Someone has to be. Most appear to have accepted its considerable risk.
“Their business model is essentially … you’re doing this massive buildout of infrastructure,” said Chaflin. “It is really quite painful from a free cashflow perspective, during the buildout.”

That infrastructure “needs to get funded with debt” Chaflin said. He emphasises that CoreWeave is not the only company doing this: it is the business model of “hyperscalers” and “neoclouds” – the companies building AI datacentres to support a future, still-theoretical AI economy.

In a US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing this summer, CoreWeave listed 18 different varieties of debt it is now paying back, amounting to roughly $35bn. In its most recent earnings, which do not break down this debt, that number is up by nearly $12bn, to $47bn.
It expects its interest payments to crest over $1bn next quarter. More than $10bn of its debt comes due next year.

title_en: Elizabeth Holmes went from a startup darling to powerful seductress – these gendered portrayals profited investors
excerpt_en: A female wunderkind, Holmes was presented an attractive prospect for investors. Later she was a presented as a dangerous siren who had lured them unawares.
body_en: Despite the countless books, podcasts, TV miniseries and documentaries, people continue to be fascinated by the fall of Elizabeth Holmes and her health-tech startup Theranos. We are now being offered a new insight into the founder through the much-hyped documentary, You Can See Everything.

The initial drama of the documentary takes places 34 days before Holmes started her 11-year prison sentence for investor fraud in 2023. In our research, we examined how Holmes was presented across promotional materials, tweets, talks and interviews over the ten year period from her initial appearance on the public stage in 2013 to the same period in which the documentary begins.

Valued at around US$9 billion (£7 billion) at its peak in 2014, Theranos claimed to have built a device that could run hundreds of lab tests from just a few drops of blood. Holmes and co-founder Sunny Balwani hid that the device could not in fact do what they said, leading to its 2018 shutdown and their convictions for investor fraud (and, in Balwani’s case, defrauding patients as well).

For many, the fascination in Holmes’s story lies in the hubris and deception of this young woman who set out to upend the multi-billion dollar diagnostic industry. But popular perspectives on Holmes obscure something important about how we view entrepreneurs, who we celebrate (or vilify) and whose interests this serves. This is something our research explores.

A highly sellable female entrepreneur In our analysis, we found that gendered stereotypes helped create an attractive female narrative around Theranos and Holmes between 2013 and 2015 that served (predominantly male) investor interests.

Holmes was introduced as a very specific kind of woman entrepreneur – confident, ambitious, authoritative. The prominent venture capitalist Tim Draper, who made his name backing companies like Tesla and was an early investor in Theranos, praised what he saw as Holmes’s entrepreneurial instincts in 2014. He said she was the first entrepreneur he know who kept quiet about her business “so that the competition wouldn’t get a chance to start … She had a winner and knew it”.
In 2015, Theranos board member and longtime Holmes supporter former US secretary of state Henry Kissinger talked about her as combining “fierce and single-minded dedication with great charm”.
Much was also made of her looks, with the media often noting she was a “young, blond, and blue-eyed” woman. She was a refreshing change from the usual men the industry pinned all its hopes on.

Holmes did present a highly sellable vision of a new Silicon Valley that welcomed and celebrated female entrepreneurs. In her 2019 book The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, tech historian Margaret O’Mara noted that Holmes’s rise coincided with growing public scrutiny of Silicon Valley’s lack of diversity, and the “tech-bro” homogeneity of the early-to-mid 2010s. At the time, the Valley was also beset by high profile gender discrimination cases.
For investors, Holmes was an attractive answer to a media problem the tech industry had and the media coverage of her rise certainly helped counter some of critics of the Valley’s “brotopia”.

But Holmes’s brand of female founder was not totally new and this also served investors. In many articles she was portrayed as the female reincarnation of the stereotypical “tech bro” – a Mark Zuckerberg with a heart or a Steve Jobs with a social consciousness.

Then there was her intentional self styling, which the media played up as symbols central to her status as a female tech-visionary. Holmes’s signature black turtle necks seemed to be a homage to the uniform of Jobs, who regularly wore an Issey Miyake black turtleneck. She was asked about it again and again, admitting in an interview with Glamour that she owned 150 of them.

Holmes’s founder uniform combined with the fact that she had dropped out of university to pursue her vision, like Jobs, Zuckerberg and Bill Gates, gave her many of the recognisable characteristics of a successful tech founder. She was like all these visionaries but with the added bonus of being a woman. This portrayal fed straight into investor interests by making Holmes at once both familiar and novel, helping her company Theranos’s value to climb to unprecedented heights.

However, when things started to turn sour, our research found that much less flattering gendered stereotypes were quickly deployed. These narratives framed Holmes’ downfall as female weakness in order to protect powerful men.
An ousted ‘villain’ Holmes was vilified, not only as a failed entrepreneur, but also as a seductress who had used specifically female charms to lead competent men astray.

According to Rolling Stone, she “lured” male investors into her fraudulent schemes. Meanwhile, the Evening Standard reported her as having “wooed” the men on her board to do her bidding. Financial journalists described how Holmes “dazzled” normally sober leaders at supermarket chains Walgreens and Safeway who then invested in her scheme.

Holmes’s board of directors – once portrayed as the “most illustrious board in US corporate history” – along with the other powerful men she was seen as having duped could now be presented as innocent victims of malicious female magic.

For investors, this villification of Holmes could help them spin their own narratives in order to preserve public trust in their abilities. They could argue that her monstrous supernatural abilities to bamboozle and manipulate were too strong for them to overcome. In this media framing, the fact that investors appeared not to have conducted basic due diligence before investing hundreds of millions of dollars was neither their fault nor a reflection of their real talent for investment. They were simply good men who wanted to help people but had been fooled by a woman playing on an emotional blind spot. They were credulous rather than gullible.

title_en: African glamour: the bold women who styled, wrote and read Drum magazine
excerpt_en: Drum’s male reporters are legendary, but women were far more involved in shaping the magazine’s content than many realise.
body_en: Drum magazine was an African institution in the 1950s and 1960s. Launched in South Africa, it would go on to publish five regional pan-African editions across eight countries.

Much has been made of the male reporters of the magazine, but a new open source book considers how women used it to shape their worldviews and opportunities. We spoke with media scholar Wanjirũ G. Mbure about Out For Glamour In Africa.

What was Drum? Initially known as The African Drum, Drum magazine started in South Africa in 1951, three years after apartheid was signed into law. The system of white minority rule would violently disenfranchise Black South Africans.

This was particularly evident in cities like Johannesburg, where large numbers of Black South Africans migrated from rural areas to work on mines. With little investment in housing and social services, they were forced to live on the outskirts of the city.

Magazines thrived in this period, looking to appeal to growing European and African urban consumers. Drum’s founder, South African sportsman turned journalist Robert Crisp, viewed it as a magazine that would connect Africans across the continent and the Black diaspora. It would preserve African traditions and identities at risk of disappearing in the face of colonial policies.

Crisp left the venture shortly after it began, and one of the magazine’s investors, Jim Bailey, took over. Under a series of carefully selected editors, Drum took on a distinctively urban quality. It gained Pan-African prominence over the next 20 years, with regional editions in west, east, and central Africa.
Read more: Journalism of Drum’s heyday remains cause for celebration - 70 years later

The magazine included feature articles of various lengths, full-colour adverts and cover images of African women, women of African descent from across the diaspora, and prominent male African political figures. Columns and photographs created by a mostly Black staff covered sports, crime, fashion, culture and politics.

Content in regional editions reflected local realities, but was similar in how women were represented. Analysing the South African and west African (Ghana, Nigeria) editions alongside the east African one (Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda) allowed me to understand the Africa-wide scope of Drum. I was interested in how advertisers shaped this outlook, how editions differed, if at all, and in how it engaged with women as contributors, subjects and readers.

So, how were women represented? Women’s representation was transnational: a shared pursuit of urban success and upward mobility in cities across Africa, the US, the Caribbean and Europe. In the 1950s, similar migratory changes are also taking place in Europe.

As wages increased in some African cities, permanent family migrations to urban areas became possible and there was a marked increase of women in cities. As their purchasing power grew, so did advertising targeting them.

With a surge of African nations attaining independence from European colonisers, cities became even more attractive. Professional opportunities grew, some cultural activities, like cinema and theatre, that had previously been reserved for Europeans became available to some Africans. New social and cultural institutions, like museums and media, were also established. These changes shifted women’s roles as they entered new urban spaces and professions.

Interconnected realities produced a new form of femininity I call “femme urbAfricana.” In it, a woman’s role in the city was reimagined as acceptable and legitimate. In Drum, there’s a focus on the different ways that women are taking part in city life, what they wear, and their connection to women outside their immediate environment who are also claiming their place in the city. Women’s appearance and appeal to the opposite sex are central. But women are also pioneers of urban culture and life.
Read more: Juby Mayet, legendary South African writer and journalist, remembered through new book

With independence, ordinary Africans were talking about national identities and their role in nation-building. Drum, for example, featured several competitions for national dresses in new countries. The magazine profiled pioneering women like Ugandan lawyer Mary Ilero-Uchong, Tanzanian athlete Theresia Dismass and South African golfer Mary Mafokeng. Several stories discussed African first ladies and politicians’ wives as ideal models of African femininity.
Drum’s reporting about the place of modern cosmetics and western fashion in definitions of African womanhood resulted in a renewed focus on beauty and fashion in the modern nation-state.

One example is a story in Drum about Gladys Nguyo, a Kenyan beauty expert and contestant in Miss Uhuru, an independence celebration pageant. After being trained in cosmetics, Nguyo became one of Kenya’s earliest beauty professionals. In the original articles submitted to Drum that I found in the archive, editorial notes downplay references to Nguyo’s consulting work for the wives of former British colonial military officials.

The editorial notes framed Nguyo as apolitical even as the magazine celebrated her position as an African urban pioneer. The original copy also referenced the ethnicity of the Kenyan women in the accompanying photos, details that were later removed. Drum positioned Nguyo’s work in cosmetics as one that fulfilled the needs of all women in a new multiracial African nation. The magazine shaped how readers understood this pioneering African woman.

How did African women contribute to and relate to the content? Black women also contributed actively to the magazine’s vision of urban life. The works of some of its women journalists, like Juby Mayet, may be familiar to readers.

Among the lesser-known women writers for Drum were African-American journalist Glenda Wina and Zimbabwe-born journalist Anne Placido. Features by women such as Kenya’s political activist Philomena Chelagat and Ghana’s dancer and writer Beryl Karikari showed that they enhanced the magazine’s appeal.

title_en: Cop31: the world is heading for climate ‘overshoot’ – the UN summit must start planning for what comes next
excerpt_en: Small island states are pushing for urgent discussions about removing carbon dioxide and deliberately cooling the planet.
body_en: Sahabi Ware / shutterstock A surprising thing has happened at the UN climate conference, Cop31, as it gears up to its conclusion in Antalya, Turkey. Negotiators are discussing how to cool the planet.

You might think this should not be surprising, but how to respond to the latest climate science was not on the agenda when the meeting started. Now, the summit’s latest draft decision explicitly recognises a role for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) alongside deep emissions cuts. This is a significant shift, driven by pressure from some of the countries most vulnerable to climate change – the small island states – in response to two alarming scientific reports in the last month.

The World Meteorological Organization has confirmed that the rate at which the Earth is heating up is accelerating. One reason is the planet is becoming less “reflective”: the loss of ice and snow, changes in cloud formation and (paradoxically) reductions in atmospheric pollution means that more solar radiation is being absorbed rather than reflected into space.

The result is that the Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5°C will not be met. There’s a new term for this new warming trajectory: “overshoot”. As a United Nations Environment Programme (Unep) report explains, the best we can hope for now is to exceed 1.5°C but then limit the extent of the overshoot, peaking emissions as soon as possible and then returning to 1.5°C later in the century.

Unfortunately, Unep also notes that this may be easier said than done. The longer temperatures remain above 1.5°C, the greater the risk of triggering irreversible changes to systems such as polar ice sheets and glaciers, ocean currents and the Amazon rainforest, which could make returning to lower temperatures impossible.

Once a rainforest is lost, it can be extremely difficult to restore – with global climate consequences. finchfocus90 Beyond cutting emissions Up until now we have thought there were basically two responses to global heating. We needed to cut emissions (mitigation), and cope with the warming we experienced (adaptation). But overshoot means that achieving net zero emissions is not enough. By the time we get there the temperature will be too high.

Overshoot will require two other kinds of response. As well as cutting the flow of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, we can physically take them out, a process known as carbon dioxide removal or CDR.

And we will also need to consider different ways to increase the planet’s reflectivity. These include limiting aircraft contrails (which trap heat), expanding the white surface areas of the earth (both buildings and crops), or making glaciers more stable. It could potentially include various methods of “ solar radiation management ”, such as brightening clouds over the oceans, or injecting reflective aerosols into the stratosphere. If any of these “climate cooling” technologies could help bring temperatures down, they need much more carefully governed research.

Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is not the same as carbon capture and storage (CCS), which refers to the capture of emissions from industrial plants before they reach the atmosphere. In all net zero scenarios CCS is needed to deal with the residual emissions of fossil fuels. But we now know CDR is going to be required as well – first alongside emissions reduction, to slow warming down, and then to return the global temperature to a safer level.

There are various potential removal methods. Some are familiar and uncontroversial, though not yet being done at anything like the required scale. These are natural processes such as tree-planting, restoring ecosystems and improving carbon in soils.

Other “novel” forms of CDR are still in development. Carbon uptake methods in the oceans include enhancing the ocean’s alkalinity and the fertilisation of phytoplankton by adding iron. On land, enhanced natural processes include adding charcoal to soils (“ biochar ”), and accelerating the creation of carbonates from rock weathering.

There are also more technological interventions. These include “bioenergy with carbon capture and storage” ( Beccs), in which biomass is burned for energy and the emissions captured and stored underground; and “direct air capture”, the removal of CO₂ from the air with advanced machines.

All of these methods are now being piloted, but remain expensive. Some of them also raise environmental risks: before any could be used at significant scale, countries would need to be sure that they would not have negative side-effects. In turn that means the world needs to think seriously about their governance.

The politics of cooling the planet But there is currently no place for such talks. Neither novel methods of carbon dioxide removal, nor increasing the earth’s reflectivity, are formally part of the Cop negotiations or indeed any other UN policy process.

This is because many countries have believed that any discussion of these would take the pressure off emissions reduction. They have been supported in this view by some of the larger climate NGOs, who have not wanted anything to distract from their campaign against fossil fuels.

But the world has changed. Climate science says emissions reduction on its own can no longer keep us on a safe climate pathway. This surely makes blanket opposition to novel CDR and cooling methods untenable. Governments need to be scaling up research into these methods and considering their governance. At the very least, they should be talking about them.

This is why the latest moves at Cop31 are so important. At this point it is not clear whether countries will agree to a statement on how to respond to overshoot. Some are still opposed. But if the final text does acknowledge that active cooling will be needed, it will mark the beginning of a new era in climate action.

title_en: We’re Publishing the Tariff Refunds the Government Has Refused to Disclose
excerpt_en: The post We’re Publishing the Tariff Refunds the Government Has Refused to Disclose appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Illustration by ProPublica. Source illustrations: Brandon Celi for ProPublica. After President Donald Trump’s “emergency” tariffs were overturned by the Supreme Court in February 2026, the government began processing billions in refunds to importers, including many recognizable public companies.

The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for. ProPublica requested the information, but U.S. Customs and Border Protection denied our requests. (We’re appealing.)
So our reporters found another way: analyzing the financial disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.

Today, ProPublica published “Cash Back,” a database of figures on refunds for tariffs paid under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. The database includes 343 public companies for which we found mentions of refunds, amounting to more than $28 billion recovered or expected.

See How Much Companies Are Getting in Tariff Refunds At least nine companies have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis published earlier this week.
Recognizable businesses include the tool company Stanley Black & Decker and the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls, and the golf equipment brand Titleist.
Many other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money.

ProPublica’s examination of tariff refunds was limited to publicly traded companies, which are required to disclose detailed financial information. None of the companies that said they are using the money for bonuses have ever said they planned to refund customers. How private companies are using their refunds is unclear because they aren’t normally required to disclose such information.

What’s included in the database? The Supreme Court ruled on Feb. 20, 2026, that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act doesn’t authorize the president to impose tariffs. The U.S. Court of International Trade ordered U.S. Customs and Border Protection to refund the duties it had collected.

This tracker covers refunds on those tariffs disclosed by publicly traded companies. Public companies must disclose events that affect their finances, such as tariff payments and refunds, on earnings calls and in regular reports filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission. We collected information from these public sources through Oct. 7, 2026.
Before publishing, we contacted all companies shown here to check the accuracy of the numbers we had found.
We grouped companies by industry using a combination of designations from Morningstar.

How did we determine refund amounts? ProPublica searched through securities filings and earnings calls using key phrases to isolate companies that mentioned tariff refunds. For each company, we created a document that included the extracted text around each phrase. For SEC filings, that included parsed Extensible Business Reporting Language when available.

We then used an open-weight artificial intelligence model for a first pass at identifying refund amounts. ProPublica reporters reviewed each company by hand to make sure our database is accurate and contacted all companies to confirm the amounts.
Companies normally record tariff refunds in their financial statements under two accounting models:

Gain contingency: when the refund has been received or recovery is essentially certain. Loss recovery: when the refund is probable and can be reasonably estimated. To determine a company’s recovered refund, we added up the amounts it recorded that were essentially certain or probable (sometimes known as “receivable”), plus the amounts it disclosed as having been received.

The government is required to pay interest on tariff amounts it is returning, at rates determined by the IRS on a quarterly basis. Companies disclosed that interest in different ways. Some reported the refund and the interest separately, while others reported a single amount that included both. When a company reported them separately, we added the interest to the refund to capture the full amount of money that a company was receiving from the government.

Some companies reported only their net refund instead of the full amount received. For example, a company might report only what was left of the tariff refund after reinvesting into its business or after passing part of the refund onto customers. In these cases, we reported the net amount. When companies reported a range, we used the lower end. In both cases, we noted that information on the company page.
The specific security filings reviewed were: 8-K, 10-Q, 10-K, 8-K/A, 10-Q/A, 10-K/A, 6-K, 6-K/A, 20-F, 20-F/A, 40-F, 40-F/A and any associated exhibits.

Can I get a refund? Only importers or the authorized custom brokers who filed the entries can submit a request for a refund. That means that even if companies passed tariff costs on to customers through higher prices, the refund goes to the company, and it is up to the company to determine how the money is used.

UPS and FedEx are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing them. The companies have set up online portals for customers to track their refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals who paid them to ship products.

Other companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers, though these companies’ customers are generally other businesses. Trade experts say these business-to-business vendors likely have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs.
